title: Short Stuff: Petrified Wood
summary: Short Stuff episode on petrified wood. Josh and Chuck open with a banter about a Mudhoney concert, then explain that petrified wood is fossilized wood in which the organic material is replaced by minerals (often silica, which forms quartz) after burial cuts off oxygen and slows decay, a process called permineralization that usually takes millions of years but can occur in as little as seven to thirty-six years under the right conditions. They discuss Gallatin National Park's stacked petrified forests in Montana, with about 2,000 vertical feet of forests layered by repeated volcanic ash burials, and mention the petrified forest in Yellowstone where logs lie fallen. They cover how minerals create colors (hematite for pink or red, native iron for green, pyrite for black), how petrified logs look like bark-covered logs dusted with silica, why they are heavy, and why they often break into clean, saw-like pieces. They note petrified wood is found worldwide and that some locations have legal protections against removal.

segments.title: Opening banter and Mudhoney shout-out
segments.summary: Chuck gives a music shout-out about seeing Mudhoney live, and the hosts make a segue into petrified wood.

segments.title: What petrified wood is
segments.summary: Josh explains petrified wood is fossilized wood that has become mineral rather than wood, and Chuck notes the process is called permineralization and usually takes millions of years.

segments.title: Fossilization timeline
segments.summary: The hosts mention a study finding petrification can happen in as little as seven to thirty-six years.

segments.title: How burial and minerals petrify wood
segments.summary: Chuck explains that burial by ash, mud or silt cuts off oxygen so decay slows, allowing minerals to seep in; Josh adds that minerals fill pores and the remaining hardened mineral, usually silica, forms quartz. Chuck notes speed depends on rapid burial or abundant minerals.

segments.title: Petrified forests in Yellowstone and Gallatin, Montana
segments.summary: Josh describes Yellowstone's petrified logs fallen into rivers and sediment, and Gallatin National Park in Montana, where upright trees were petrified in place by repeated ash burials, forming about 2,000 vertical feet of stacked forests.

segments.title: Colors, appearance and weight
segments.summary: Chuck describes how minerals fill pores to create colors and patterns; Josh lists hematite (pink or red), native iron (green), and pyrite (black). Josh notes silica dust on bark and that petrified wood is much heavier than wood.

segments.title: Worldwide distribution and brittle fractures
segments.summary: Chuck notes petrified wood is found worldwide wherever trees grew, and that laws restrict taking it. Josh explains it is brittle and often snaps cleanly, looking sawed.
